Harden the destination check itself: resolve the hostname and reject the request if any resolved address is loopback, link-local (169.254.0.0/16), or private, and pin the connection to the validated address to close the DNS-rebinding window between the check and the connect.

findings.title: writeStaged/stagePath create a predictable temp file without O_EXCL, allowing symlink-following overwrite
findings.evidence: stagePath (edgeproxy/cache.go:25-27) builds the scratch filename as `filepath.Join(os.TempDir(), "edgeproxy-stage-"+key+".part")`. os.TempDir() is the world-writable shared temp directory (/tmp unless TMPDIR overrides it), and `key` is not a secret: it is the SHA-1 of the caller's own request parameters (edgeproxy/cache.go:18, fed from edgeproxy/handlers.go:49), so any party who knows or can choose the request can compute the exact path offline. writeStaged then opens that path at edgeproxy/cache.go:33 with `os.OpenFile(path, os.O_WRONLY|os.O_CREATE|os.O_TRUNC, 0o644)` -- no O_EXCL, no O_NOFOLLOW, and no check that the entry is a regular file the process owns. Because O_CREATE without O_EXCL happily opens an existing symlink by following it, an attacker who pre-plants /tmp/edgeproxy-stage-<key>.part as a symlink to any file the service user can write causes that target to be truncated to zero and overwritten with the streamed image bytes. The comment at edgeproxy/cache.go:22-24 explicitly designs for path reuse across retries, which is what makes the pre-planting window arbitrarily wide. promote() at edgeproxy/cache.go:51 then os.Rename()s that path into the cache directory, so the same planted entry also lets an attacker steer what lands in the cache. The 0o644 mode also makes the staged bytes world-readable, unlike the 0o750 used for the cache directory at edgeproxy/cache.go:47. Reachability note: as of this revision writeStaged, stagePath and promote have no callers anywhere in the repository (verified by grep), so the flaw is dormant until the cache-write path is wired into thumbHandler. [Stage 8 (critic): CONDITIONAL_VIABLE — Intrinsic flaw (Rule 08) but writeStaged/stagePath have zero call sites; the symlink-overwrite primitive is latent until the staging path is wired back into the handler.]
findings.impact: A local attacker sharing the temp directory with the process (co-tenant container in the same mount namespace, sidecar, or any other local account) can truncate and overwrite any file writable by the edgeproxy user -- the configuration file, cached objects, or logs -- and can substitute the content that promote() moves into the cache directory. The world-readable 0644 staged files additionally leak fetched image content to other local users.
findings.recommendation: Stage inside a directory the service owns rather than the shared temp dir -- e.g. a 0700 subdirectory of cfg.CacheDir created with os.MkdirAll before use -- and create the scratch file with os.CreateTemp(stageDir, "edgeproxy-*.part") so the name is unpredictable and the open is O_EXCL by construction. If a deterministic name is genuinely required, add os.O_EXCL to the OpenFile flags and unlink the leftover on retry after verifying with os.Lstat that it is a regular file owned by the process. Tighten the mode from 0o644 to 0o600.

findings.title: Session cookie configured with httpOnly:false and secure:false in config/default.json
findings.evidence: The session cookie options are read verbatim from config at orderdesk/server.js:41 (`cookie: config.get('session.cookie')`), and orderdesk/config/default.json:12-17 sets `"httpOnly": false` (orderdesk/config/default.json:15) and `"secure": false` (orderdesk/config/default.json:16) with a 24-hour `maxAge`. These are not express-session's defaults - `httpOnly` defaults to true - so both protections were explicitly turned off. `httpOnly:false` exposes the `odsid` session id to `document.cookie`, and there is a live script-injection sink in the same app at orderdesk/lib/render.js:61. `secure:false` lets the browser transmit the session id over plaintext HTTP. `app.set('trust proxy', 1)` at orderdesk/server.js:21 means the app sits behind a proxy, so a TLS-terminating front end will not compensate: the cookie is still emitted without the Secure attribute and will be attached to any http:// request for the domain.
findings.impact: Session identifiers are stealable by any XSS payload (the stored-XSS path at orderdesk/lib/render.js:61 makes this concrete, not theoretical) and by any passive network observer or captive-portal/hostile-Wi-Fi attacker who can induce one plaintext request to the console domain. Either yields a 24-hour authenticated session as the victim merchant user, with full access to that tenant's orders.
findings.recommendation: Set `"httpOnly": true` and `"secure": true` in orderdesk/config/default.json (keeping `sameSite: "lax"` or tightening to `"strict"`), and allow `secure:false` only through a local-development override file, never in the default. If any front-end code genuinely reads the cookie, move that state to a separate, non-authenticating cookie.

findings.title: Unpinned wildcard dependency "node-fetch": "*" in package.json
findings.evidence: orderdesk/package.json:25 declares `"node-fetch": "*"`. Every other entry in the dependency block uses a caret range with a floor (orderdesk/package.json:19-27, e.g. `"express": "^4.19.2"`), so this one is a clear outlier rather than a convention. `*` matches ANY published version with no lower or upper bound: a fresh install resolves to whatever is latest at that moment, which silently crosses major versions and, more importantly, means a compromised or maliciously published release of `node-fetch` (or of anything it pulls in transitively, since its own tree is likewise re-resolved) is installed automatically the next time the lockfile is regenerated or the package is installed without one. Because the build already executes remote code at install time (orderdesk/package.json:16), there is no reviewed checkpoint that would catch the substitution.
findings.impact: A single malicious or hijacked `node-fetch` publish executes in the application process and at install time, with access to the DB credentials read at orderdesk/lib/db.js:17, the webhook HMAC secret read at orderdesk/routes/webhooks.js:32 and all order data. Uncontrolled resolution also makes builds non-reproducible, so the compromised version cannot be identified after the fact by reading the manifest.
findings.recommendation: Pin to a bounded range consistent with the rest of the manifest (e.g. `"node-fetch": "^2.7.0"`, or drop the dependency entirely since Node >=20.11 per orderdesk/package.json:8 ships a global `fetch`). Commit package-lock.json, install with `npm ci`, and add a CI check that fails on any `*`/`latest`/unbounded specifier plus `npm audit --audit-level=high`.

findings.title: Session fixation: /api/auth/login never regenerates the session id
findings.evidence: The login handler at orderdesk/server.js:59-86 assigns identity onto the EXISTING session object - orderdesk/server.js:80 `req.session.userId = user.id;` and orderdesk/server.js:81 `req.session.merchantId = user.merchant_id;` - without first calling `req.session.regenerate()`. A repo-wide grep for `regenerate` returns no hits anywhere in the tree. Consequently the pre-authentication session identifier is promoted to an authenticated one: whatever `odsid` value the browser presented before login keeps working, now carrying `userId`/`merchantId`. `saveUninitialized:false` (orderdesk/config/default.json:11, read at orderdesk/server.js:40) does not help - the attacker's chosen sid is persisted at the moment login writes to it. Delivering a chosen sid to the victim is easy in this app: the cookie is not httpOnly (orderdesk/config/default.json:15), the signing secret needed to forge a valid signature is public (orderdesk/config/default.json:9), and the cookie is not Secure (orderdesk/config/default.json:16) so it can be set from a plaintext sibling origin.
findings.impact: An attacker who can plant a cookie in the victim's browser before login (via the stored XSS at orderdesk/lib/render.js:61, a subdomain, or an active network position) holds a session id that becomes fully authenticated the instant the victim signs in - complete account takeover of the merchant console with no credential theft and nothing visible to the victim. `req.session.destroy` on logout (orderdesk/server.js:89) closes the window only after the fact.
findings.recommendation: Regenerate before assigning identity: wrap the assignment in `await new Promise((ok, ko) => req.session.regenerate(e => e ? ko(e) : ok()));` and only then set `req.session.userId` / `req.session.merchantId`, saving before responding. Fix the enabling conditions too (httpOnly/secure cookie flags and the hardcoded secret).

findings.title: _check_url() https-only guard is applied only to the initial URL; urlopen follows redirects to http:// and ftp:// unchecked
findings.evidence:
`download()` validates the scheme exactly once, before the request is made: `_check_url(url)` at packmate/packmate/fetch.py:41, which enforces `parts.scheme in ALLOWED_SCHEMES` == `{"https"}` (fetch.py:31-33, ALLOWED_SCHEMES at fetch.py:17). The actual transfer then runs through `urlopen(req, timeout=60)` (packmate/packmate/fetch.py:52), which installs `urllib.request.HTTPRedirectHandler` by default and transparently follows up to 10 redirects. The final URL is never re-validated -- `resp.url` is not inspected anywhere in `download()` (fetch.py:52-66).

`HTTPRedirectHandler.http_error_302` only rejects schemes outside `('http', 'https', 'ftp', '')` (verified against the local CPython 3.12 source). So an `https://` URL that clears `_check_url` can be 302'd to `http://` or `ftp://`, and packmate will download the bundle over cleartext -- exactly the outcome the docstring at fetch.py:26-30 claims is impossible ('file://, ftp:// and plain http:// are all refused here before urlopen sees them'). The same unvalidated redirect also permits redirection to an internal-network or link-local host (SSRF-style reach) from a registry the operator only intended to talk to over the public internet.

Untrusted ingress: the URL comes from the lockfile or from `--registry` (packmate/packmate/cli.py:64, 103 -> `registry_url`, fetch.py:69-71); the redirect target is chosen entirely by the remote registry. This composes badly with the fact that the digest check is optional (see the separate integrity finding) and with the RCE/traversal primitives in the extract and manifest paths: after the downgrade an on-path attacker can swap the bundle bytes and nothing downstream will notice.

Note for completeness: TLS certificate verification itself is *not* disabled -- no `ssl` context or `ssl._create_unverified_context` is used anywhere, so the first hop is properly verified. The defect is strictly that the scheme guard does not survive redirection.
findings.impact: A malicious or compromised registry (or one whose CDN/mirror is hijacked) can force packmate onto plain HTTP or FTP for the bundle body, dropping all transport authentication and integrity; an on-path attacker then substitutes a bundle that triggers the manifest-deserialisation RCE or the zip-slip write. The same redirect can be aimed at internal-only hosts, letting a remote registry pivot packmate into the operator's private network.
findings.recommendation: Re-validate after the redirect chain: keep `_check_url` as a pre-flight, and additionally assert `_check_url(resp.url)` on the opened response before writing any bytes (packmate/packmate/fetch.py:52), aborting with `FetchError` on a downgraded or off-host final URL. Better, install a custom `HTTPRedirectHandler` subclass in a dedicated `OpenerDirector` whose `redirect_request` rejects any non-https target (and optionally any host change), instead of relying on the module-level default opener.

findings.title: Bundle integrity verification is optional and never enforced: download() skips the digest check on an empty pin and the parsed lockfile digests are only counted
findings.evidence:
packmate looks like it verifies downloaded and installed bundles, but no code path actually does.

1. `download()` computes a SHA-256 while streaming (packmate/packmate/fetch.py:50, 56) but the comparison is short-circuited by the truthiness of the pin: `if expected_sha256 and got != expected_sha256.lower():` (packmate/packmate/fetch.py:61). An empty string silently disables verification entirely rather than failing closed.

2. That empty string is the default. `cmd_pull` calls `download(url, expected_sha256=args.sha256 or "")` (packmate/packmate/cli.py:66) and `--sha256` defaults to `""` (packmate/packmate/cli.py:104). So the ordinary `packmate pull <name> <version>` accepts whatever bytes the registry returns, unverified.

3. The pinned-digest machinery is inert. `cmd_install` parses the lockfile with `load_lockfile(workdir)` (packmate/packmate/cli.py:44 -> manifest.py:71-86), and the resulting dict is then used exactly once -- for its length in a log line, `len(lock)` at packmate/packmate/cli.py:56. No digest in it is ever compared against any file. Repo-wide grep confirms `load_lockfile` has no other caller.

4. `verify_payload()` is named like an integrity check but only tests `(root / entry).exists()` (packmate/packmate/manifest.py:93); it detects a truncated bundle, never a tampered one.

The result is a control that reads as implemented and reviews as implemented, but that a user relying on 'packmate pins digests' does not actually have. Combined with the redirect downgrade in the fetch path, the transport guarantee can also be removed, leaving zero verification of the artifact that is then fed to the deserialising manifest parser and the unguarded zip extractor.
findings.impact: Any party able to serve or substitute the artifact -- a compromised registry, a mirror, a caching proxy, or an on-path attacker once the fetch has been downgraded to http -- can deliver an arbitrary bundle that packmate installs without complaint, and the lockfile the operator believes pins it is never consulted. Given the manifest-deserialisation RCE and the zip-slip write in the same package, a swapped bundle is directly equivalent to code execution on the installing host.
findings.recommendation: Fail closed rather than silently skipping: make the digest mandatory in `download()` (drop the `expected_sha256 and` short-circuit at packmate/packmate/fetch.py:61 and raise `FetchError` when no pin is supplied, with an explicit opt-out flag such as `--no-verify` if one is genuinely needed), and validate the pin's shape (64 hex chars) before comparing. Wire the lockfile in: have `cmd_pull` look up the pin for `name`/`version` and pass it to `download`, and have `cmd_install` hash each payload file and compare it against the corresponding lockfile entry, extending `verify_payload` beyond an existence test. Prefer `hmac.compare_digest` for the comparison as defence in depth. For real supply-chain assurance the pin must be carried out-of-band (or signed), not read from inside the bundle it is meant to attest.

findings.title: Terraform plan file containing sensitive values is published as a workflow artifact (`tfplan-${{ github.run_id }}`)
findings.evidence:
platform-infra/.github/workflows/deploy.yml:52-57 uploads `terraform/tfplan` - the binary plan produced at deploy.yml:50 - as a workflow artifact with a five day retention. A Terraform plan file stores the fully resolved attribute values of every resource in cleartext; HashiCorp documents that plan files are not encrypted and must be treated as secret material. Here that concretely includes the RDS master credential, which is a string literal in the configuration (`password = "Pg-orderdesk-2024-rotate-me"`, platform-infra/terraform/rds.tf:45), plus the value of `TF_VAR_db_master_password` supplied from `secrets.DB_MASTER_PASSWORD` (deploy.yml:48) and the account id exposed via the `account_id` output (platform-infra/terraform/main.tf:115-117).

The `sensitive = true` marking on the variable (platform-infra/terraform/variables.tf:42) only suppresses console rendering; it does not redact the plan file, and GitHub's secret masking does not apply to the contents of an uploaded binary artifact. The exposure surface is wide because the `plan` job runs on `pull_request_target` (deploy.yml:6) for fork PRs, so plans are produced and uploaded on outsider-initiated events, and workflow artifacts of a public repository are downloadable by anyone through the Actions API.
findings.impact: Anyone who can list artifacts on this repository - every member/collaborator with read access, and the whole internet if the repository is public - can download `tfplan-<run_id>` within the retention window and recover the production Postgres master password and the full resolved infrastructure state. Combined with the database being reachable from the internet (rds.tf:49 `publicly_accessible = true` and rds.tf:20 allowing 5432 from 0.0.0.0/0), that credential is directly usable for a remote login to production data with no further foothold.
findings.recommendation: Stop passing the plan between jobs as an artifact: run plan and apply in the same job against the same checkout, or store the plan in an encrypted, access-controlled location (S3 with SSE-KMS and a short lifecycle) and pass only its key. If a plan must be surfaced for review, upload only the sanitised `terraform show -json | jq` output with sensitive attributes stripped, never the raw `-out=` file. Remove the credential from the configuration entirely (see the hardcoded-password finding) so no plan can ever carry it.

findings.title: ECS task role granted `s3:*` on the artifacts bucket, including bucket-policy, ACL and public-access-block writes
findings.evidence:
platform-infra/terraform/iam.tf:21-38 grants the application task role `actions = ["s3:*"]` (iam.tf:25) on both `aws_s3_bucket.artifacts.arn` and its `/*` object path (iam.tf:27-30). The comment at iam.tf:19-20 claims the task 'needs the whole s3 verb surface on its own bucket (multipart uploads, tagging, lifecycle probes), but only from inside the VPC endpoint'. Checking that against the actual arguments: the `aws:SourceVpce` condition (iam.tf:32-36) is genuinely present, but it constrains only the NETWORK PATH of the call, not the set of operations. The task runs inside the VPC, so every one of its calls satisfies the condition - the condition does nothing to limit what the task may do to the bucket. The stated need (multipart, tagging, lifecycle probes) is a handful of object-level verbs; `s3:*` is roughly a hundred, including the bucket-level configuration verbs the comment does not mention.

Concretely, `s3:*` on the bucket ARN includes `s3:PutBucketPolicy`, `s3:PutBucketAcl`, `s3:PutObjectAcl`, `s3:PutBucketPublicAccessBlock`, `s3:DeleteBucketPolicy`, `s3:PutBucketVersioning`, `s3:PutBucketLogging` and `s3:DeleteBucket`. `PutBucketPolicy` in particular is a privilege-escalation primitive: the task can author a resource policy granting a principal it controls - or `Principal: "*"` - full access, escalating beyond what its own identity policy allows and beyond the VPC-endpoint boundary the comment relies on, since a resource policy has no such condition. `PutBucketLogging` lets it sever the access-log flow to `aws_s3_bucket.logs` configured at platform-infra/terraform/s3.tf:97-101, destroying the audit trail.
findings.impact: An attacker who achieves code execution in the application container (SSRF to the task metadata endpoint, RCE, or a dependency compromise) escalates from 'read/write the app's own objects' to 'own the bucket': rewrite the bucket policy to grant themselves or the world persistent access from outside the VPC, tamper with the build artifacts and storefront assets that the CDN and the warehouse tablets fetch (a downstream supply-chain foothold, made worse by the bucket already being public-read at s3.tf:34), turn off access logging to hide it, or delete every object.
findings.recommendation: Split the statement in two: object-level verbs (`s3:GetObject`, `s3:PutObject`, `s3:DeleteObject`, `s3:AbortMultipartUpload`, `s3:ListMultipartUploadParts`, `s3:GetObjectTagging`, `s3:PutObjectTagging`) on `"${aws_s3_bucket.artifacts.arn}/*"`, and bucket-level read verbs (`s3:ListBucket`, `s3:ListBucketMultipartUploads`, `s3:GetBucketLocation`) on the bucket ARN. Never grant `s3:PutBucketPolicy`, `s3:PutBucketAcl`, `s3:PutObjectAcl`, `s3:PutBucketPublicAccessBlock`, `s3:PutBucketLogging` or `s3:DeleteBucket` to a runtime workload. Keep the `aws:SourceVpce` condition as defence in depth, but do not treat it as the authorisation boundary.

findings.title: Debug enabled by default makes the global exception handler return exception text and full stack traces
findings.evidence: pulse-api/app/settings.py:68 hardcodes `debug: bool = True` with no _env() override, in a Settings object whose environment already defaults to 'production' (settings.py:48). The global handler registered for every unhandled Exception at pulse-api/app/main.py:96-103 branches on that flag and, when true, attaches `str(exc)` and `traceback.format_exc()` to the 500 response body (main.py:100-102). The same flag also forces application-wide DEBUG logging at main.py:20-23. The path is reachable by an unauthenticated caller: current_user parses claims from an unverified token and, outside its try/except (which only catches jwt.PyJWTError, auth.py:69), calls `int(claims["sub"])` at auth.py:76 and `int(claims.get("org", 0))` at auth.py:78 - a token payload with a missing or non-numeric `sub`/`org` raises KeyError/ValueError, which escapes as a 500 carrying the full traceback instead of a 401. A malformed `exp` at auth.py:72 does the same.
findings.impact: An unauthenticated attacker gets absolute source paths, module and function names, local frame context and library versions for the running service, plus raw driver error text (including fragments of SQL and connection details) whenever a database exception surfaces - mapping the internals and greatly accelerating exploitation of the injection sinks in routes_invoices.py:51 and routes_admin.py:57.
findings.recommendation: Default debug to False and derive it from the environment (`debug: bool = _env_bool("PULSE_DEBUG", False)`), never enabling it when settings.environment == 'production'. Return only an opaque error id to the client and keep the traceback in the server log. Separately, catch KeyError/ValueError around the claim coercion in auth.py:72-80 and raise 401 instead of letting it become a 500.

findings.title: require_admin performs no tenant binding, letting an admin of one org act on any org in org_stats and sync_ledger
findings.evidence: require_admin (pulse-api/app/auth.py:83-86) only asserts that the caller's role is in {admin, owner} (User.is_admin, auth.py:26-28); it carries no notion of which tenant that admin belongs to, even though every User is created with an org_id (auth.py:22, auth.py:78) and roles are stored per user row alongside org_id (main.py:78, main.py:87-92). Two admin routes are addressed by a tenant identifier taken from the URL and never compare it against `admin.org_id`: org_stats accepts `org_id` at routes_admin.py:32 and passes it straight to count_invoices at routes_admin.py:38, and sync_ledger accepts `org_id` at routes_admin.py:85 and interpolates it into the outbound ledger call at routes_admin.py:90 while attributing the action to the caller (`requested_by: admin.email`, line 91). The module docstring's claim that these are 'mounted behind the ops VPN' (routes_admin.py:1) is not enforced anywhere in the application - the router is mounted unconditionally at main.py:37.
findings.impact: A customer-side admin or owner of tenant A can read invoice volume for any other tenant (business intelligence leak, and an oracle for enumerating valid org ids) and can trigger ledger synchronisation for tenant B's invoices, causing unauthorised state change in the downstream ledger service attributed to the wrong operator.
findings.recommendation: Separate the two role families: keep a tenant-scoped admin check that asserts `org_id == admin.org_id` on every /orgs/{org_id}/... route, and gate genuinely global back-office operations on a distinct staff/superuser claim that customer accounts can never hold. Do not rely on network placement (ops VPN) as the only tenant boundary.

findings.title: Agent containment limits declared in config.yaml (limits.max_steps, limits.tool_output_chars) are never read; planner.py hardcodes MAX_STEPS
findings.evidence:
config.yaml presents a `limits` block that reads as the operator's containment control for the agent loop: `max_steps: 8` at deskagent/config.yaml:20 and `tool_output_chars: 8000` at deskagent/config.yaml:21, under the heading at deskagent/config.yaml:19. Neither key is ever read. I grepped the whole corpus for 'max_steps', 'MAX_STEPS', 'tool_output_chars' and 'limits': the only hits are the config.yaml declarations themselves and the unrelated constant at deskagent/agent/planner.py:24 (`MAX_STEPS = 8`), which is a module-level literal consumed at deskagent/agent/planner.py:92 (`for step in range(MAX_STEPS)`). The output cap is likewise a bare literal, sliced at deskagent/agent/planner.py:120 (`output[:8000]`) and deskagent/agent/planner.py:115 (`output[:2000]`). load_config (deskagent/agent/server.py:22-24) parses the file and create_app (deskagent/agent/server.py:31-35) consumes only state_dir, model, max_tokens, api_key_env and service_token_env; `limits` is silently dropped, and run_turn's signature (deskagent/agent/planner.py:79-85) has no parameter through which a configured value could be threaded.

The same defect affects the ticket source: deskagent/config.yaml:15-17 declares `tickets.index: "agent/data/tickets.json"` and `refresh_minutes: 15`, but search_tickets hardcodes the location at deskagent/agent/tools.py:83 (`Path(__file__).resolve().parent / "data" / "tickets.json"`) and no refresh logic exists anywhere. So an operator can repoint the agent's retrieval corpus in configuration and the running system will keep reading the old file.

This is a protection-mechanism failure rather than an injection: the control appears to exist, is the obvious knob to reach for during an incident, accepts any value without error, and has no effect. Because the loop bound and the tool-output cap are exactly the two levers that limit blast radius once a prompt injection has taken hold (deskagent/agent/planner.py:92-124), an operator responding to an incident by setting `max_steps: 1` would believe the agent was contained while it continued to take eight tool-using turns per request. [Stage 8 (critic): CONDITIONAL_VIABLE — The hardcoded values happen to equal the config values today, so the drift is latent: the control only fails when an operator tightens config.yaml and believes it took effect.]
findings.impact: Security configuration that silently does nothing. An operator tightening `limits.max_steps` or `limits.tool_output_chars` to contain a misbehaving or injected agent gets no change in behaviour and no warning: the loop still runs 8 tool-executing iterations per request (deskagent/agent/planner.py:24,92) and still returns 8000 characters of raw tool output into the model context (deskagent/agent/planner.py:120). Likewise, repointing `tickets.index` after discovering a poisoned ticket corpus has no effect, because deskagent/agent/tools.py:83 keeps reading the original path — and that corpus is the source of the untrusted text that gets promoted into the system prompt at deskagent/agent/planner.py:75. The result is a false belief about the system's containment state during exactly the situation where accurate belief matters.
findings.recommendation: Wire the configuration through, or delete the keys so they cannot mislead. Read cfg['limits'] in create_app (deskagent/agent/server.py:27-35), pass max_steps and tool_output_chars into run_turn as parameters, and replace the literals at deskagent/agent/planner.py:24, 115 and 120 with those values; read cfg['tickets']['index'] and pass it to search_tickets instead of the hardcoded path at deskagent/agent/tools.py:83. Then add a startup validation step that fails loudly on unknown or unused configuration keys, so a knob that no code consumes can never again be silently accepted.

findings.title: cacheKey derives cache identifiers with SHA-1 over attacker-controlled input
findings.evidence: edgeproxy/cache.go:18 computes the cache identifier as `sha1.Sum([]byte(fmt.Sprintf("%s|%d|%s", target, width, format)))`, with crypto/sha1 imported at edgeproxy/cache.go:4. The `target` operand is fully attacker-controlled: it arrives from the query string at edgeproxy/handlers.go:49, which forwards the raw `url`, `origin` and `key` parameters read at edgeproxy/handlers.go:17. The resulting digest is the security boundary between cached objects -- it is the filename used by promote() (edgeproxy/cache.go:50), by lookup() (edgeproxy/cache.go:59) and, indirectly, by the unauthenticated /raw endpoint (edgeproxy/handlers.go:73-79), so two inputs that hash alike are one cache entry. SHA-1 is collision-broken (SHAttered, and practical chosen-prefix collisions since 2020), and here the attacker controls both preimages and can pad them freely because `target` is an arbitrary-length string. [Stage 8 (critic): CONDITIONAL_VIABLE — cacheKey is live (handlers.go:49) but its output only names cache entries that are never written; SHA-1 collision resistance matters once cache writing is restored.]
findings.impact: An attacker who computes a SHA-1 collision between two distinct upstream targets can make the proxy store one object under the identity of the other, poisoning the cache with content of their choosing or reading another object's cached bytes -- the same outcome as a cache-key confusion, but reachable even after the delimiter ambiguity is fixed. Independently, the SHA-1 dependency is a compliance and future-proofing liability for a value that gates content identity.
findings.recommendation: Replace crypto/sha1 with crypto/sha256 (or blake2b) in cacheKey and truncate the hex digest if a shorter filename is wanted; a 256-bit hash truncated to 128 bits still resists collision search. Update the import at cache.go:4 and any operational tooling that assumes 40-hex-character cache filenames.

findings.title: Cache key collision in thumbHandler: url, origin and key concatenated without a delimiter before cacheKey
findings.evidence: edgeproxy/handlers.go:49 builds the cache identity as `cacheKey(q.Get("url")+q.Get("origin")+q.Get("key"), width, format)` -- three independently attacker-controlled query parameters (read from r.URL.Query() at edgeproxy/handlers.go:17) concatenated with no separator and no escaping, then hashed at edgeproxy/cache.go:17-19. Distinct request tuples therefore collapse onto one key. Concretely: `?url=https://uploads.example.net/a&key=b` and `?url=https://uploads.example.net/ab` both produce the preimage 'https://uploads.example.net/ab' even though the first fetches object /a and the second fetches /ab -- note that in the url branch (edgeproxy/handlers.go:42) the `key` and `origin` parameters are not used for the fetch at all, yet they still steer the cache key, giving the attacker a free primitive to mint any cache identity they like for whatever content they caused to be fetched. The same ambiguity spans branches: `?origin=assets&key=.example.net/x` and `?url=https://assets.example.net/x` are different upstream requests whose concatenations can be made to coincide. The colliding key is then used to serve bytes verbatim at edgeproxy/handlers.go:50-54 without any re-verification that the stored object corresponds to the requested target. [Stage 8 (critic): CONDITIONAL_VIABLE — The collision is unambiguous in cacheKey construction, but no code path in the tree populates the cache (writeStaged/promote have zero call sites), so lookup() at handlers.go:50 cannot hit today. Viable the moment cache writing is restored or the directory is filled out-of-band.]
findings.impact: Cache poisoning and cross-object content confusion: an attacker can bind content they control (or an object they are allowed to read) to the cache slot of a different object, so subsequent victims requesting the legitimate object are served the attacker's bytes, and conversely an attacker can address another tenant's cached object on uploads.example.net. Note that today the promote()/writeStaged() writer functions at edgeproxy/cache.go:31-55 have no callers, so nothing populates the cache directory and the lookup branch at handlers.go:50 never fires -- the defect is latent until the cache-write path is wired up, which the code plainly intends.
findings.recommendation: Key the cache on the single canonical value that actually determines the fetched bytes -- the resolved upstream URL returned by resolveKnownOrigin / validated in fetchRemote -- not on a bag of raw query parameters. If several fields must be combined, serialize them unambiguously (length-prefixed, or a JSON/struct encoding, or a hash-of-hashes) so no two distinct tuples share a preimage, and include every field that affects the stored bytes (width, format, resolved URL) explicitly. Store the resolved target alongside the cached object and verify it matches on lookup before serving.

findings.title: Cache-hit path in thumbHandler reflects the upstream-controlled Content-Type instead of the transformed format
findings.evidence: On a cache miss the handler sets the response type from the validated, server-chosen format: `w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "image/"+format)` at edgeproxy/handlers.go:64, where `format` was allowlisted to webp/jpeg/png at edgeproxy/handlers.go:29-32. On a cache hit the handler instead echoes `ctype` at edgeproxy/handlers.go:52 and writes the cached bytes at edgeproxy/handlers.go:53. That `ctype` is the raw `resp.Header.Get("Content-Type")` returned verbatim by the upstream at edgeproxy/fetch.go:90, assigned into the handler at edgeproxy/handlers.go:40/42 -- i.e. a header value chosen by whatever server answered the fetch. Because the upstream destination is itself attacker-selectable through the SSRF at edgeproxy/fetch.go:64, the attacker controls this header end to end and can set it to text/html, application/javascript, or any other renderable type while the body served is the cached object rather than the freshly fetched one. This is a trust-boundary violation: the origin's header is promoted into the proxy's own response without validation, and it contradicts the type the miss path would have produced for the identical request. [Stage 8 (critic): CONDITIONAL_VIABLE — Reached only on the cache-hit branch, which never fires because nothing in the tree writes cache entries.]
findings.impact: The proxy can be made to serve stored bytes under an attacker-chosen Content-Type on its own origin. With a polyglot cached object (a valid PNG/JPEG whose bytes also parse as HTML) this becomes stored cross-site scripting in the edgeproxy origin, and more generally it defeats any downstream assumption that /thumb only ever returns images. Preconditions: a populated cache entry, which the current revision never creates because promote()/writeStaged() (edgeproxy/cache.go:31-55) have no callers -- so this is latent alongside the rest of the cache path.
findings.recommendation: Never propagate the upstream Content-Type. Set `"image/"+format` on the cache-hit branch exactly as the miss branch does at handlers.go:64, or persist the server-derived type with the cached object and replay that. Add `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` and a `Content-Disposition: attachment` default on /raw (edgeproxy/handlers.go:84) so mislabelled bytes cannot be rendered inline.

findings.title: SQL statement injection through migration filename in applyMigration
findings.evidence: orderdesk/lib/db.js:57-66 builds a mysql client invocation whose `-e` payload is a formatted string: orderdesk/lib/db.js:62 passes `` `source ${file}` `` where `file` is `path.join(__dirname, '..', 'migrations', path.basename(fileName))` (orderdesk/lib/db.js:58). The doc comment at orderdesk/lib/db.js:52-56 claims safety because 'execFile keeps the arguments out of a shell either way'. Verified: that half is true - `execFile` spawns without a shell, and `path.basename` does neutralise directory traversal (confirmed: `path.basename('../../etc/passwd')` returns `'passwd'`). But the comment reasons about the wrong parser. The `-e` value is interpreted by the MySQL CLIENT, which splits its argument on `;` into multiple statements; `path.basename` preserves `;`, spaces and quotes. A filename such as `001_init.sql; DROP DATABASE orderdesk; --` therefore yields `-e "source /.../migrations/001_init.sql; DROP DATABASE orderdesk; --"`, executing attacker-chosen SQL as the migration DB user. Reachability today: `applyMigration` is exported at orderdesk/lib/db.js:68 but a repo-wide grep finds no caller (the `migrate` script at orderdesk/package.json:15 points at `scripts/migrate.js`, which does not exist in the tree), so this is a latent injection primitive that arms itself as soon as the runner is written over a directory listing or a CLI argument. [Stage 8 (critic): CONDITIONAL_VIABLE — applyMigration has no caller in the tree and the filename comes from a directory listing, so there is no untrusted ingress today; retained under Rule 08 as an intrinsic statement-injection path in the module's own logic.]
findings.impact: Anyone who can influence a filename in the migrations directory - a contributor, a compromised CI checkout, an upload path, or a future caller that passes a user-supplied name - executes arbitrary SQL with the migration account's privileges, which for schema work is typically DDL/DROP-capable: full database destruction or silent backdooring of the schema (e.g. inserting an attacker-controlled row into `users`).
findings.recommendation: Do not interpolate the path into a client statement. Feed the file to the client on stdin (`execFile('mysql', [...], {input: fs.readFileSync(file)})` via spawn, or shell-free redirection), or read the file in Node and run its statements through the existing pooled connection. Additionally allow-list the filename against a strict pattern such as `/^[0-9]{3,}_[a-z0-9_]+\.sql$/` and reject anything else, and correct the misleading comment at orderdesk/lib/db.js:52-56.

findings.title: Non-constant-time password digest comparison and login timing oracle in /api/auth/login
findings.evidence: Two defects in the same comparison block. (1) orderdesk/server.js:75 compares the derived key with a plain JavaScript string operator: `if (!user || digest !== user.password_hash)`. `!==` on strings short-circuits at the first differing character, so the comparison is not constant time; the secret-derived value at orderdesk/server.js:72 is verified with a data-dependent operation, while the same file already imports `node:crypto` (orderdesk/server.js:4) and the codebase demonstrably knows the correct primitive - `crypto.timingSafeEqual` is used for the webhook HMAC at orderdesk/routes/webhooks.js:48. (2) The expensive PBKDF2 at orderdesk/server.js:71-73 is computed ONLY when a user row was found (`const digest = user ? crypto.pbkdf2Sync(password, user.salt, 120000, 32, 'sha256')... : null`). 120,000 SHA-256 iterations take tens of milliseconds, so the 401 response for a known email is dramatically and reliably slower than for an unknown one - a remotely measurable account-existence oracle with no authentication required. The email is also written to the log line at orderdesk/server.js:76.
findings.impact: An unauthenticated attacker can enumerate valid console accounts at scale by timing 401 responses (the difference is milliseconds, well above network noise for a repeated-sample attack), producing a target list for credential stuffing and phishing. The non-constant-time digest comparison additionally leaks a per-character timing signal about the stored PBKDF2 output during verification.
findings.recommendation: Always perform the KDF, using a fixed dummy salt and a throwaway comparison when no user row was found, so both branches cost the same. Compare with a length-checked `crypto.timingSafeEqual(Buffer.from(digest, 'hex'), Buffer.from(user.password_hash, 'hex'))` instead of `!==`. Use the async `crypto.pbkdf2` rather than `pbkdf2Sync` so the KDF does not block the event loop, and consider migrating to scrypt/argon2id.

findings.title: ECS task role trust policy has no `aws:SourceAccount`/`aws:SourceArn` condition (aws_iam_policy_document.task_assume)
findings.evidence:
platform-infra/terraform/iam.tf:3-12 defines the trust policy for `aws_iam_role.task` (iam.tf:14-17): it allows `sts:AssumeRole` (iam.tf:5) for the service principal `ecs-tasks.amazonaws.com` (iam.tf:7-10) with no `condition` block whatsoever. AWS's IAM guidance for service-linked task roles calls for pinning the trust to the calling account and, ideally, the specific task-definition ARN via `aws:SourceAccount` and `aws:SourceArn`, specifically to address the confused-deputy problem where the ECS service is induced to hand the role's credentials to a workload the role owner did not intend.

The contrast within the same file is telling: the task's permission policy immediately below does add a condition (`aws:SourceVpce`, iam.tf:32-36), so conditions are understood here - the trust document simply has none. This is a hardening gap rather than a standalone break-in: with no cross-account `iam:PassRole` path, exploitation requires a principal that can already register a task definition and call `ecs:RunTask` in this account. It is reported because it removes the only account-scoped guard on a role that holds `s3:*` over the artifacts bucket (iam.tf:25).
findings.impact: Any principal in the account that can register an ECS task definition and run a task - a much larger set than 'the orderdesk service', and a set that includes anyone who reaches the `*:*` deployer role - can attach this role to a container of their choosing and inherit its `s3:*` grant on the artifacts bucket, with nothing in the trust policy tying the role to the intended task family or account. It also removes the documented defence against the ECS confused-deputy pattern.
findings.recommendation: Add a condition block to `data.aws_iam_policy_document.task_assume` pinning `aws:SourceAccount` to `data.aws_caller_identity.current.account_id` and `aws:SourceArn` (ArnLike) to `arn:aws:ecs:${var.region}:${account_id}:*`, narrowed to the specific cluster/task-definition ARN where possible, mirroring the conditional style already used for the artifacts policy at iam.tf:32-36.
